state.case_summary:
A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. On examination, he had left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5) without meningeal signs. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL). Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. 

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

root.label: Subacute Progressive Multifocal Neurological Deficit with Fever and Increasing Intracranial Pressure
supporting_facts: positive urine toxicology for benzodiazepines and opiates
hypodense area in the right basal ganglia on noncontrast head CT
T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule on brain MRI
increased intracranial pressure on lumbar puncture
excluded_candidates: Toxic or metabolic encephalopathy due to benzodiazepine or opiate use: less likely due to presence of focal neurological deficits and imaging findings
Infectious encephalitis: less likely due to negative CSF studies for common pathogens
CNS vasculitis: less likely due to absence of systemic symptoms and negative laboratory studies
salient_findings: hypodense area in the right basal ganglia
T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule
